entry.title: Transactions, Deadlocks & Log Based Recovery
entry.summary:
Transactions, Deadlocks & Log-Based Recovery – Hands-on SQL Demo
**Databases are powerful because they ensure data integrity even when multiple users access the system at the same time. This is managed through transactions, deadlock detection, and log-based recovery. In this blog, I demonstrate these concepts using a single Accounts table in Oracle Live SQL.** We first create a table to simulate account balances: INSERT INTO Accounts VALUES (1, 'Alice', 1000); COMMIT;
Goal: Transfer ₹500 from Alice to Bob. Rollback before commit to ensure no partial update. UPDATE Accounts -- Rollback the transaction -- Check balances (should be unchanged)
✅ Balances remain: Alice → 1000 Lesson: Atomicity ensures that either all operations in a transaction succeed, or none do. Goal: Simulate a deadlock between two sessions. Session 1: Lock Alice’s account and try to update Bob’s. Session 2: Lock Bob’s account and try to update Alice’s.
🔥 Oracle detects circular wait → deadlock → one session is rolled back automatically. Lesson: Deadlocks can occur when two transactions wait on each other’s locks. DBMS automatically resolves them. Goal: Show that updates are tracked for recovery using logs. -- Rollback -- Verify
✅ Even after rollback, balances are restored, demonstrating undo capability via internal logs. Note: In Oracle Live SQL, redo/undo logs are internal. The rollback proves that log-based recovery works. 🎯 Summary Special thanks to @santhoshnc Sir for guiding us to try these experiments hands-on in Oracle Live SQL.

entry.title: Symmetric/Asymmetric Encryption
entry.summary:
Symmetric Encryption
Example: Person A encrypts a document with a shared secret key/passphrase. Person B needs the same key to decrypt it. Problem: The challenge is how to share the secret key securely. If A emails the passphrase to B, anyone intercepting that email can also decrypt the document. This is called the key distribution problem. Secure key sharing methods: Or, better: use asymmetric encryption to send the key securely.
Two keys are used: a public key and a private key. Keys come in pairs and are mathematically linked: Public key: shared openly, used for encryption. Private key: kept secret, used for decryption. Person B shares their public key with Person A. Advantage: No need to send secret keys via insecure channels. Even if someone intercepts the public key, they cannot figure out the private key. In practice:
Then, symmetric encryption (which is faster) is used to encrypt the actual large file or communication. This is exactly how TLS/SSL (HTTPS) works: Your browser and the server exchange public keys. They use asymmetric encryption to safely share a symmetric session key. That symmetric key is then used for fast, secure communication.
